blocks.text: Functional group interconversion (FGI) means changing one functional group into another, as needed to synthesise a particular compound. FGI plays a crucial role in designing routes to target molecules: simple starting materials can be converted into more complex targets using FGIs as building blocks, and FGI helps both to create the carbon skeleton and to choose the route. The interconversions met in earlier chapters are summarised below.

blocks.alt: Map of interconversions between two-carbon compounds: alkene H2C=CH2, halogenoalkane CH3-CH2-Br, amine CH3-CH2-NH2, aldehyde, alcohol CH3-CH2-OH, amide, ester, carboxylic acid and acid halide, with reagents on the arrows: HBr, KOH (alcohol), NH3, Heat/H2SO4, H2O/H2SO4, PBr3, KOH (aq), K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, NaBH4, V2O5, LiAlH4, C2H5OH/H+, SOCl2.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.3: Functional group interconversion in aliphatic organic compounds (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.3).

blocks.alt: Benzene in the centre: CH3Cl/AlCl3 up to toluene; SO3/H2SO4 left to benzene sulfonic acid, then (i) NaOH (ii) HCl down to phenol; HNO3/H2SO4 right to nitrobenzene, then Sn, HCl down to aniline; ethanoyl chloride/AlCl3 down to acetophenone. Toluene gives benzyl alcohol with (i) Cl2, light (ii) KOH(aq) and benzoic acid with KMnO4/H2SO4.
